title: Davutoglu Dissolves Future Party as Opposition Consolidates, Turkey-Syria Open Central Bank Accounts, US-Saudi Strikes Hit Iraq
subhead: Former PM Davutoglu's exit from party politics clears the field for Ozel's Yeni Parti, while CBRT Governor Karahan's Damascus visit formalizes banking ties with Syria's new government — and US-Saudi joint strikes in Iraq complicate Ankara's delicate Iraq balancing act the day after al-Zaidi's visit.

sections.heading: Davutoglu Dissolves Future Party, Exits Opposition Politics
sections.body:
Former Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu announced Wednesday he is stepping away from party politics and dissolving his Gelecek (Future) Party, according to Daily Sabah. The move removes a small but symbolically significant opposition actor from Turkey's political landscape at a moment when the opposition is already in flux — Ozgur Ozel's Yeni Parti launch this week has reshuffled parliamentary allegiances, and the CHP remains divided between reformists and Kemalists.

Davutoglu, who founded Gelecek in 2019 after breaking with Erdogan's AKP, never translated his foreign policy stature into electoral success. His departure accelerates a broader consolidation: center-right opposition voters now face a simpler choice between the AKP establishment and the emerging Yeni Parti bloc. Whether Ozel absorbs Gelecek's infrastructure and local networks — or simply inherits its voters — remains to be seen.
sections.whyItMatters: Davutoglu's exit removes the last prominent AKP dissident with his own party platform, concentrating the opposition into fewer poles and giving Ozel's Yeni Parti a clearer lane — but also more pressure to deliver.

sections.heading: CBRT Governor Visits Damascus, Opens Syria Correspondent Account
sections.body:
Central Bank of Turkey Governor Fatih Karahan traveled to Damascus on Wednesday, where he signed an agreement with Central Bank of Syria Governor Mohammad Raslan to open an official Syrian central bank account with the CBRT, SANA reported. The account is designed to facilitate bilateral financial and commercial transactions between the two countries.

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani met Karahan separately to discuss expanding economic and financial cooperation. The meeting also addressed the withdrawal of the Turkish lira from northern Syria and efforts to help Syrian banks establish correspondent accounts in Turkey, according to SANA. A supervisory director at the Syrian central bank described the CBRT as an 'important correspondent institution' given existing trade ties.

The banking deal coincides with a milestone in Syria's monetary transition: July 30 is the deadline for exchanging old Assad-era banknotes, after which they cease to be legal tender. The Central Bank of Syria says approximately 80% of old currency has been exchanged since the redenomination process began in January, which lopped two zeros off the old pound. The new Syrian pound still trades at roughly 13,000 old pounds to the dollar, The Media Line reported.
sections.whyItMatters: The CBRT's formal banking relationship with Syria's new authorities institutionalizes an economic integration that has been building informally for months — and the Turkish lira withdrawal discussion signals Ankara's push to monetize its influence in northern Syria through official channels.

sections.heading: US-Saudi Strikes Hit Iran-Backed Militias in Iraq, Complicating Ankara's Calculus
sections.body:
US Central Command and Saudi Arabian forces conducted their first publicly acknowledged joint strikes against Iran-backed militia sites in eastern Iraq on Tuesday, according to CENTCOM. The strikes targeted militia infrastructure after Houthi drones out of Yemen and Iran-backed militia drones out of Iraq hit Saudi oil facilities within a 24-hour span, part of a broader barrage of over 30 IRGC-directed drone attacks on regional targets.

The timing is sensitive for Ankara. Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi had just left Ankara after talks with Erdogan when the strikes hit. Zaidi, who emerged as a consensus candidate after months of political deadlock, pledged to disarm non-state armed groups by end of September — a deadline even he acknowledged would be challenging, given that the most powerful militias have refused to lay down arms. Zaidi ordered security agencies to investigate the Saudi attacks, and the Iraqi military stated Iraq is committed to 'preventing Iraqi territory from being used as a route or launching point for any attack targeting brotherly or friendly countries.'

The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias, denied responsibility and described the Saudi claims as 'fabrications,' implying the attacks were Houthi in origin. The group warned that 'any foolish Saudi action will be met with a harsh response.'
sections.whyItMatters: The US-Saudi escalation inside Iraq directly intersects with Turkey's energy and security interests — Zaidi's disarmament pledge is now being tested by force, and Ankara's Kirkuk stake and pipeline negotiations depend on Iraqi stability that these strikes could destabilize.

sections.heading: Iraq-Turkey Pipeline Framework Expires Without Replacement
sections.body:
The 1973 Iraq-Turkey Crude Oil Pipeline Agreement formally expired on July 27, and Zaidi's visit to Ankara on July 28 ended without a replacement pipeline deal, Upstream reported. Erdogan said Turkey aims to sign a 'comprehensive energy cooperation agreement as soon as possible,' and Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar indicated a twelve-month cover text was near final to keep oil flowing to Ceyhan during broader negotiations.

But the gap between the old framework's expiry and a new agreement is legally significant. A Forbes analysis by Guven Yildiz notes that the 1973 treaty became 'the legal battlefield' of the Kurdistan Regional Government's independent marketing fight with Baghdad — an ICC tribunal in 2023 found Turkey had breached the pipeline agreements by facilitating Kurdish exports without federal consent, with the net award to Iraq clustering around $1.5 billion before interest. Any new framework must be written under that shadow.

The TPAO stake in Kirkuk — 15% of BP Energy Company of Kirkuk Limited, alongside BP at 43% and ConocoPhillips at 42% — is the concrete gain. It covers more than 3 billion barrels of oil equivalent in initial development across Baba, Avanah, Bai Hassan, Jambur, and Khabbaz fields. But as Yildiz argues, 'fifteen percent is not control. It is incorporation' — Turkey converts geography into a bookable seat beside Anglo-American capital, under Iraqi title.
sections.whyItMatters: The expired framework leaves Kirkuk-Ceyhan flows in a legal grey zone covered only by a temporary arrangement. The real story is not the '1 million barrels/day' political number but TPAO's equity seat — Turkey is shifting from transit middleman to upstream stakeholder in Iraq's northern oil.

sections.heading: Syria's Displaced Kurds Still Blocked from Return, Turkish Influence Cited
sections.body:
Tens of thousands of Kurds displaced by Turkey's 2019 offensive in Ras al-Ain remain stranded in camps near Hasakeh, Al-Monitor reported, despite a January deal between the Syrian Democratic Forces and Damascus to integrate Kurdish institutions. While returns to Afrin (site of the 2018 Turkish operation) have proceeded, Ras al-Ain residents are still blocked by Turkish-backed fighters squatting in their homes.

Displaced camp resident Ahmad Oussi told Al-Monitor that former fighters call them saying 'You can't go back to our homes... they're our homes now.' A Kurdish authorities' representative in Damascus described Ras al-Ain returns as one of the deal's 'main outstanding issues requiring implementation.' Jawan Isso, from a committee representing displaced people, said 'significant obstacles' remain, citing the security situation and noting the town 'is still under Turkish influence.' According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, Turkish troops maintain three positions in the Ras al-Ain area.

The impasse exposes the gap between Ankara's diplomatic normalization with Syria's new authorities and the reality on the ground: Turkey's military presence and proxy fighters continue to block the return of displaced populations that Damascus has agreed should go home.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's normalization with Damascus means little to displaced Kurds if Turkish-backed forces still occupy their homes. The Ras al-Ain impasse is a live test of whether political agreements can override military facts on the ground.

sections.heading: Oil Prices Slide as US-Iran Pause Frays, Red Sea Disruption Deepens
sections.body:
Oil prices slid below $90/barrel on Wednesday, Reuters reported, as the US-Iran pause created space for diplomacy — but the calm was short-lived. By Wednesday, US and Saudi forces struck Iran-backed militia sites in Iraq, while Iran launched renewed missile attacks on American forces in the region. France 24 described the renewed bombardment as ending 'nearly a week of relative calm and dimming hopes for diplomacy.'

Separately, Houthi drone attacks on Saudi oil installations and Red Sea shipping disruptions have intensified. Ship traffic through Bab el-Mandeb fell after the attacks, per Kpler shipping data, adding to the existing Hormuz disruption. The overland route through Syria is absorbing some of the slack: 2.1 million tonnes of Iraqi fuel have moved to Europe by road since April, with daily truck counts growing from 10 to 1,000, according to MSN reporting on Syrian transit data.

For Turkey, the dual chokepoint disruption — Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb — makes the Kirkuk-Ceyhan corridor and the proposed Basra-Haditha pipeline even more strategically valuable. But the near-term reality is that oil price volatility and supply chain disruption continue to pressure the Turkish economy, which remains exposed to energy import costs.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey sits at the intersection of every energy chokepoint crisis — and every alternative route. The dual disruption of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb raises the strategic premium on Ceyhan, but short-term oil price swings still hit Ankara's inflation fight.

bottomLine: Three stories define the day: Davutoglu's dissolution of the Future Party consolidates the opposition into fewer poles and clears Ozel's path; CBRT Governor Karahan's Damascus visit formalizes Turkey-Syria banking integration just as Syria's old currency expires; and US-Saudi strikes in Iraq, hours after Zaidi left Ankara, expose the fragility of Turkey's Iraq energy bet — the pipeline framework has expired with no replacement, and the militia disarmament Zaidi promised is being tested by force. The regional picture is darkening again: the US-Iran pause that briefly pushed oil below $90 has shattered with new strikes and counter-strikes, and dual disruption at Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb keeps Turkey's Ceyhan corridor at the center of energy geopolitics — and its inflation outlook at the mercy of oil price volatility.
sources: Daily Sabah, SANA (Syrian Arab News Agency), Al-Monitor, Forbes (Guven Yildiz), AP, Upstream Online, BP Press Releases, Reuters, France 24, CENTCOM, The Media Line, Alhurra/MBN Iran Briefing, MSN
